problem: A particle $P$ of mass $1\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $6\sqrt{x}\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, and the particle has velocity $v=2\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ at $x=1,$ calculate the velocity of the particle at $x=4.$
worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}6\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{x}^{3/2}{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =4(8-1) \\  & =28\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=2\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ at $x=1.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{1}$ at $x=4$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 28 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot {v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot (2\sqrt{2})^{2} \\ 28 & =\frac{1}{2}{v}_{1}^{2}-4 \\ \frac{1}{2}{v}_{1}^{2} & =32 \\ {v}_{1}^{2} & =64 \\ {v}_{1} & =\pm 8.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=4$ is $8\,m/s.$
